Excellencies, let me begin by thanking the co-chairs of the Preparatory Committee of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development for convening this fourth session of the PrepCom. First, Zimbabwe reaffirms its strong commitment to multilateralism and to the full implementation of the 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals. Second, we cannot depend on a global financial architecture that was established for a world that existed 80 years ago. The current system is falling short and cannot meet today's development needs. We must therefore urgently reform the global financial architecture so that it is inclusive and reflective of today's global realities. It must include debt restructuring mechanisms that are timely and fair. It must guarantee affordable concessional financing, especially for developing countries. In this regard, Zimbabwe underscores the importance of ensuring debt sustainability through enhanced debt transparency, responsible borrowing and lending practices, and the operationalization of effective debt workout mechanisms that place development goals at the center. Third, Zimbabwe calls for stronger international cooperation to combat illicit financial flows, which continue to deprive developing countries of critical resources for development. We must enhance global efforts to strengthen tax cooperation, improve transparency, and curb profit shifting and tax evasion. Fourth, we stress that unilateral coercive measures undermine the right to development, particularly for countries already facing structural vulnerabilities. Such measures must be lifted to allow affected countries to fully participate in and benefit from the global economy. Finally, We are encouraged that the draft outcome document recognizes the need to address the diverse needs and challenges faced by countries in special situations, including African countries and landlocked developing countries. I wish to assure you of Zimbabwe's constructive engagement throughout the process. I thank you.

In Honduras, we are in favour of a nimble, fair, renewed financial architecture promoting more inclusive global economic governance, ensuring equal financing conditions for developing countries with access to concessional financing and effective mechanisms for debt sustainability. To do this, we suggest doing the following. Two, we need to overcome austerity. The macro economy must improve people's lives and financial institutions must be sensitive to social realities and our development realities. We need to have economic stability with social justice that supports national efforts to achieve the sustainable development goals. Three, the use and mobilisation of resources must be based on equity, social justice and the protection of our common good, guaranteeing the rights to development and national sovereignty. We support access to additional financing and innovative financing, recognizing the value both of public and private sources of financing. Four, we need to reform the risk assessments in international financial regulations because current standards penalize investment in the global south. The Basel Committee and other financial organs must work with institutions of the south to establish criteria that recognize our realities, capacities, and development opportunities. We also need to review the role of credit rating agencies whose practices limit access to financing. We support the establishment of an annual dialogue which is structured and of high level under the aegis of ECOSOC to ensure greater transparency and accountability. We believe that financing for development must be critically linked to the upholding of all human rights. It is not enough to speak about economic efficiency. We need to focus on dignity, equity and social justice. In this regard, the final declaration must clearly reflect a commitment in this regard. The new global framework that will be adopted in Seville must facilitate access to innovative financial resources. It must support a root and branch reform of the international financial architecture, and it must urgently close the gap that prevents genuinely sustainable development.

While entirely bridging our differences may not be realistic for every theme, the legacy of the summit will depend on success on certain topics. To this end, we should set ourselves actionable and achievable goals. Few themes are as influential in determining countries' capacity to develop than debt and fiscal space. Managing debt and liquidity challenges remain vital. To this end, we must recognize and build on existing relevant international processes like the common framework and the three-pillar solution and strive for their improvement and increased transparency. This includes strengthening countries' capacity to borrow responsibly and sustainably. In this regard, I would like to acknowledge the work of the African Legal Support Facility. Furthermore, we remain convinced that private capital holds tremendous untapped potential. FFD4 should push for broad action in this realm. Together, we should strive for long-term engagement with investors, develop sustainable value chains and open investment opportunities. The Kingdom of the Netherlands seeks more attention for approaches focused on systemic innovation without the use of scarce ODA. Initiatives like the Dutch-based ILX Fund set up to engage pension funds into investing into a development portfolio underscore this potential. Finally, I would like to draw your attention to a critical point. The action agenda should focus should fully recognize and include women, girls, and marginalized groups. Empowering these groups will help us harness growth and development beyond what has already been achieved. It's not only the right thing to do, it is the smart thing to do. I thank you.

I thank His Excellency the Vice Minister for International Cooperation of the Netherlands, and I now give the floor To Her Excellency Ms. Doris Uzoka Anyite, the Minister of State for Finance of Nigeria.

At the outset, let me express our profound gratitude and appreciation to the co-chairs and all vice-chairs of the preparatory process of the FFD4. for their dedicated efforts towards ensuring that we negotiate an outcome document that is responsive to the needs of member states, especially developing ones, in the face of the widening SDG financing gap estimated to be about 4 trillion annually. For Nigeria, the main pillars of a renewed financing framework for sustainable development must be anchored on increased domestic resource mobilization, through which developing countries can raise more revenue to meet critical development needs and of course pay back their debt. Increased tax revenues through broadening of the tax base and plugging loopholes that aid tax avoidance, evasion, and other profit shifting by multinational is an important step in this regard, while the use of technology in the taxation process will guarantee transparency and accountability. Nigeria expects the outcome document to extract commitments to extend support to developing countries in their tax modernization process, as well as commitments towards international cooperation in tax matters. that ensure legal loopholes between jurisdictions are blocked. In this regard, we expect that the FF4 outcome document will give renewed impetus to ongoing negotiations for a framework convention on international cooperation in tax matters. Furthermore, Nigeria also strongly supports the development of efficient, standardized domestic and global beneficial ownership registries, as these are positive steps towards increased domestic resource mobilization. Nigeria is hopeful that the FFD4 will give renewed attention to longstanding problems of illicit financial flows, which have denied countries, especially developing countries, of much needed resources for sustainable development. We expect also that the outcome document will pay attention to the need for speedy return of illegally removed assets to countries of origin. Co-chairs, even though there have been some positive outcomes, we have heard time and again of the need for a reform of the global financial architecture, as the current system has failed to meet the legitimate developmental aspirations of much of the world's developing countries. Nigeria expects that the FF4 document will also commit to decisive resolution of the debt crisis by addressing unsustainable debt levels in developing countries, including through debt swaps, moratoriums, debt forgiveness and cancellations, and concessional lending for development, and as a forward-looking solution, provide some more involvement and framework for private sector participation. We expect also that due attention is paid to the call for a more representational global financial architecture that accommodates the aspirations of developing countries to have bigger voices in the international financial institutions towards ensuring that they are more inclusive, equitable, just, and responsive.
I thank her excellency, the Minister of State for Finance of Nigeria, And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iraq, who will speak on behalf of the G77 and China.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. At the outset, the group wishes to reaffirm the critical importance of this meeting as a step toward shaping an ambitious, balanced and actionable outcome for the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. We meet at a time of profound global challenges, particularly for developing countries, a world facing deepening inequalities, rising poverty, increasing geopolitical tensions, climate risks, and widening SDG financing gap, now estimated at over $4 trillion annually. For the group, a renewed global financing for development framework must respond to these urgent realities with bold commitments and practical solutions that reflect the need and aspirations of developing countries. We wish to highlight three fundamental priorities. The current system has failed to deliver adequate, predictable and equitable financing for sustainable development. The Group of 77 and China called for inclusive and transparent reform of the governance of international financial institutions, including the IMF and the World Bank, to ensure the developing countries have a stronger and meaningful voice and representations. This includes reforming the global financial safety net, improving access to special drawing rights, and revisiting global financial regulations to decrease the cost of capital for the global south. In this regard, the group underscores the important role of the United Nations in global economic governance as the most universal and inclusive multilateral forum. Number two, the widening financing gap continues to undermine our collective ability to achieve the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. Bridging these gaps requires the fulfillment of ODA commitments of 0.7 percent of GNI by developed countries in accordance with their longstanding obligations. In addition, there is a need for scaled up and better aligned South-South cooperation, which should complement and not replace North-South financial flows, which should complement -- excuse me. Effort must also be intensified to support debt sustainability through fair, timely, and development-oriented debt restructuring mechanisms. Number three, any renewed framework must respect national development priorities, policy space, and right of each country to pursue its own path to sustainable development in line with the United Nation Charter and the outcomes of Monterrey, Doha, and Addis Ababa. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iraq and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Barbados who will speak on behalf of CARICOM. I thank you co-chair.

Co-chairs, excellencies, colleagues, I have the honor to deliver these remarks on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean Community. This statement is aligned with the statement just delivered by the distinguished representative of Iraq on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. Excellencies, colleagues, CARICOM countries require strategic, targeted financial support to address the unique challenges we face in achieving sustainable development. Like other small island developing states, the colliding planetary crises of climate, biodiversity loss and pollution, and the long-lasting impacts of exogenous economic fluctuations are exacerbating our special circumstances. CARICOM therefore attaches high importance to the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, and we reaffirm our support for a fair and inclusive outcome that caters to the emerging needs of developing countries, with particular attention to small island developing states. The outcome must demonstrate international solidarity, advance bold action, and tangible deliverables to address the ongoing and anticipated financing challenges, such as those relating to scale, access, and debt, as well as persistent systemic issues. For CARICOM, tailored CIDS solutions must address not only our current, but our projected realities. They must align with our sustainable development objectives to foster social equity, environmental protection and long-term prosperity, including through economic diversification with emphasis on growth sectors like the cultural and creative industries. And they must include decisive steps to reform the international financial architecture and to strengthen the voice of representation of our countries in international financial decision-making. In closing the over four trillion dollar SDG finance gap, it is imperative that FFD4 agrees to a more inclusive financial system for growth and development for the benefit of all. It must ensure that public international development finance is scaled up to accelerate progress, particularly for developing countries, towards the achievement of the sustainable development goals. Distinguished co-chairs, the challenges that confront us globally demand that partnerships, collective action, and support take a comprehensive approach to financing, integrating development, climate, and nature in the financial system to build resilient financing mechanisms that promote sustainable development. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Barbados. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bangladesh.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. We also thank the distinguished speakers for the thoughtful introductory remarks. FFD4 is taking place at a time of multiple and interconnected crises. such as climate change and rising geopolitical tensions, and the deepening development financing gap currently standing at a staggering 4 trillion USD. We are navigating a moment of profound global uncertainty, and our reliance on multilateralism is being constantly tested. In this context, we welcome the ambition in the first draft of the outcome document to establish a renewed global financing framework. It rightly acknowledges the need for an increased investment in social protection, infrastructure and human development. But without a concrete mechanism for financing these commitments, We risk further widening the gap between our promises and delivery. Excellencies, we call for a pathway for continued economic support for graduating LDCs in line with the DPOA and Resolution 67/221 on smooth transition. To make graduations irreversible and sustainable, international support measures must be extended for a period commensurate with the development situation of the graduating countries. These supports should only be withdrawn in a staggered manner, not all at once. Prevailing illicit financial flows and repatriating stolen assets to their rightful owners are critically important to promote economic justice and equitable wealth distribution, the outcome document must address this issue adequately. Many developing countries remain burdened by external debt, stringent conditionalities and asymmetries in the global economic governance. We therefore call for delinking concessional finance from conditions that undermine domestic priorities. We appreciate the inclusion of gender equality and investment in the care economy, but beyond mainstreaming, developing countries need fiscal and monetary policy to

support the care economy.

I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh for his statement. And I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Hussain Imran Abdul Mohamed, Minister of State for Finance and Planning of the Maldives.

Thank you, Chair. The success of FFD4 will be determined by three issues. First, it must be action-oriented without concrete outcomes that can result in meaningful and tangible actions, whether long-term or short-term, we will not be able to achieve the sustainable development we seek to achieve. We cannot continue business as usual when we know that it is unsustainable. Second, it must provide a holistic response to the debt crisis unsustainable debt has meant that many developing countries are spending more on debt servicing than on their sustainable development. This is not acceptable. This is why Maldives has proposed an innovative debt relief for resilience building mechanism that rewards countries for their investment in resilience building by providing much needed debt relief. It creates the necessary fiscal space to allow developing countries to build their resilience and achieve their development goals. It allows creditors to support developing countries to invest in greener, more sustainable and more resilient development, and most importantly, it does not create new debt. Third, it must bring reform. For many developing countries, especially for small island developing states like the Maldives, the existing systems are unfit to meet our development aspirations. The FFD4 outcome document must usher in much needed reform to the international financial architecture to enable it to address the needs of developing countries and to better prepare to address new technologies and challenges. We are confident that If member states work together, we will be able to achieve these outcomes. It will be a win for multilateralism and a win for sustainable development. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished excellency, the Minister of State Finance and Planning of the Maldives and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of India.

Thank you, Chair. India appreciates the efforts of the co-facilitators and the secretariat in preparing the first draft of the FFD4 outcome document. While India aligns itself with the statements made by G77, we would like to make the following remarks in our national capacity. As we move towards Seville, it is essential that we adopt a financing framework that is consensus-based, balanced, inclusive, and responsive to the developmental priorities of all countries, especially developing countries. To that end, we propose five key pillars for a renewed global financing framework. First, strengthening the financing capacity of MDBs is fundamental to enable them to better support countries in achieving the SDGs. Scaling up their lending capacity through fresh capital infusion, implementing capital adequacy frameworks, and leveraging innovative financing mechanisms to mobilize private investment can provide the necessary impetus to financing the SDGs. Second, developed countries must fulfill their ODA commitments, ensuring allocations align with recipient countries' specific needs and national development plans and strategies. Third, strengthening the implementation of the common framework and fostering early information sharing, particularly around debt sustainability assessments, will be key to ensuring debt treatments are timely, fair, and development-aligned. Fourth, efficient mobilization of domestic resources through a combination of progressive growth-oriented domestic tax policies, as well as robust international cooperation with full respect to tax sovereignty and enhancing cooperation in curbing illicit financial flows. Fifth, promoting financial inclusion through digital public infrastructure and leveraging emerging technologies to improve the lives of citizens. Additionally, we underscore the urgent need to scale up SDG investments through concessional, long-term, and counter-cyclical financing from MDBs. Creating an enabling environment for private sector through streamlined regulations, legal safeguards, and fiscal incentives can unlock innovative and large-scale impactful financing for sustainable development initiatives. Further, strengthening international collaboration while safeguarding development, developing countries policy space to pursue their own sustainable development pathways and priorities is critical to building a more inclusive and equitable international financial architecture. Chair, India reaffirms its unwavering commitment to advancing the 2030 agenda and to working with all partners to build a fairer, more resilient and development focused global financing system. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of India. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belarus, followed by Vietnam, Jamaica, the Republic of Korea, Cote d'Ivoire, Chile, the United Republic of Tanzania. Belarus, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. The delegation of Belarus, first and foremost, would like to express its gratitude to the co-coordinators for the provision of the annotated draft of the outcome document for the fourth FFD conference and for coordinating the work on its approval. This document, in the very near future, will be the basis for comprehensive collective actions to solve urgent problems facing the modern world. and it's important that it reflects the priorities and needs of developing countries while ensuring a just and balanced approach supporting the principles of multilateralism and international cooperation. As a middle-income country that is landlocked, Belarus is convinced of the need to adopt urgent measures to ensure the varied and particular needs in development for not only countries in special situations but also MICs are taken into account. This category of countries, MICs, requires particular attention from the UN development system and IFIs so as to strengthen their national capacity to mobilize domestic resources and to access various types of external financing. There is also a need to develop transparent measures to evaluate sustainable development progress that go beyond GDP. We must not put off reform of the international financial architecture, access for developing countries to long-term financing and must be made easier. They must have access to technical assistance programmes, which must be improved, as well as technology transfers and capacity building. Developing countries and their special circumstances must be accounted for. Official aid for development must become the main channel for international cooperation, which is complementary to national efforts. The use of unilateral coercive measures run counter to international law and the goals and principles of the UN Charter must end as they are a serious barrier for the development of those countries against which they are imposed. Returning to the 2030 Agenda, we hope that discussion during the fourth session of the PrepCom will contribute significantly to the development of effective measures to respond to current and to new development issues. This must mobilize all stakeholders and available resources so as to leave no one behind. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Belarus. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Palau, will be speaking on behalf of a group of countries.

Distinguished co-chairs, I have the honor to deliver the following statement on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, AOSIS. I align these remarks with those delivered by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and China. As we embark on our fourth session, the importance of this process can't be overstated. Every day we face seismic shifts in the global international financial landscape. Multilateralism as a vehicle for hope and cooperation is constantly under threat. For those of us who rely on multilateralism and cooperation, this period of uncertainty places the smallest and most vulnerable among us, like small island developing states, at risk. This is why the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development must be more than a meeting. It must be a turning point. Over the next few weeks, EOSIS will continue to work constructively to deliver a renewed global framework for financing for development that's inclusive, equitable, effective, and transformative by, one, scaling up new and additional financing for the implementation of the 2030 agenda, including mobilization of ocean finance to achieve SDG 14, Two, advance the use of the multidimensional vulnerability index to ensure access to grants and tailored support, moving beyond income-based metrics. Three, strive for a multilateral trading system that promotes economic growth and development in developing countries, particularly in SIDS, and adopt urgent and effective measures to eliminate unilateral course of economic measures. Four, reforming the international debt architecture. architecture to be more inclusive, to support long-term resilience as well as immediate debt relief, and five, democratizing global decision-making to give SIDS greater representation and a stronger voice in shaping the international financing system. In closing, distinguished co-chairs, EOSIS doesn't come to this moment seeking charity. We're calling for justice, partnership, and a global system that delivers for all. We look forward to expanding on these issues during the intersessional consultations. The decisions we make now will determine whether the smallest and most vulnerable can not only survive, but thrive in the decades ahead. Let's rise to this challenge together. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Palau. I now give the floor to Vietnam.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, in the face of growing geopolitical uncertainty, the climate risk and widening global inequalities, the enhanced and proactive international cooperation is essential. We look forward to an ambitious outcome document and believe that more coordinated collective action in resource mobilization will bring shared prosperity. Allow me to highlight several key points. First, domestic resource mobilization alone is insufficient to meet today's urgent development challenges. We underscore the importance of international support and a reformed global financial architecture that enhance the voice and participation of developing countries. We urge multilateral development banks to simplify lending procedures to improve access to financing and allied support with national priorities and legal frameworks. We know some inconsistencies in the draft outcome document between calls for greater flexibility and the emphasis on stringent standards which makes MDB less flexible. Second, we support strong emphasis and commitment to promoting science, technology and innovation in light of rapid technological advancements, particularly in AI and digital transformation, accelerated technology dissemination is vital to reducing inequalities, lowering investment costs and achieving the SDGs. Third, Vietnam calls for the timely, widely committed contribution from developed partners, especially for climate actions and SDG implementation. Domestically, Vietnam is committed to continue fiscal reform, increasing budget efficiency and transparency, expanding the tax base and managing public finance prudently. On expenditures, we prioritize infrastructure investment, private sector engagement, FDI, and public-private partnerships as key drivers of sustainable growth. Vietnam is strongly committed to net zero emissions by 2050 and continues to invest in green growth and innovation to close development gaps. We stand ready to cooperate with all partners to ensure equitable access to development financing and to contribute constructively to a consensus-based and responsive outcome document. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Vietnam, and I will now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Jamaica. The floor is yours.

Distinguished co-facilitators, excellencies, delegates, Jamaica aligns with the statements delivered by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and China, Barbados on behalf of the Caribbean community, and Palau on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island Developing States. As noted by Senator the Honorable Camina Johnson Smith, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade of Jamaica, the eighth meeting of ECLAC's Forum of Latin American and Caribbean countries held in March 2025 in Chile, our susceptibility to climate change and exogenous shocks are exacerbated by an international financial architecture that is lopsided and provides limited protection to indebted countries. While yeoman's efforts have been made by Jamaica to build fiscal resilience, one climatic event can erode the gains made. Therefore, international support and partnerships are essential if we are to ensure that no country is left behind. We therefore anticipate that FFD4 will build on the Addis Ababa Action Agenda by adopting a renewed global framework to deliver on the SDGs. For Jamaica, a renewed global framework is one that facilitates the implementation of innovative financing mechanisms that support financial inclusion for developing countries, as well as improved access to concessional financing and climate finance at the scale required to meet our needs. It will also facilitate greater participation of developing countries in international economic decision making, the use of the MVI by MDBs and IFIs to take into account the special situation of SIDS, It would also ensure the inclusion of climate resilient debt clauses in loan agreements and facilitate the disbursement of loans in local currencies to address the cost of financing. Private sector inclusion will also be critical to success. These policy shifts are some of the measures that will provide our countries with the fiscal space needed to rebound from natural disasters and attain the SDGs. Let us collectively work towards these objectives. so that all countries can grow, thrive, and respond to crises in a resilient manner. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Jamaica, and I will now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. First, I would like to express my appreciation to the co-facilitators, Mexico, Nepal, Norway, and Zambia, as well as the UN Secretariat for their efforts in compiling and circulating the comments on the first draft. For the sake of time, I'll try to be concise and submit the full version to the Secretariat. Today, development cooperation is under pressure from growing geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, and climate change among other things. In response, it is essential to enhance both the volume and effectiveness of development finance, reform the global financial architecture, strengthen domestic policy frameworks, and uphold a rules-based multilateral trading system. Korea is scaling up its role as a responsible donor with a 65% increase in its ODA budget over the past three years. To mobilize sustainable finance, we must close financing gaps through innovative solutions, catalyze private capital, and promote digital inclusion and financial literacy. Korea remains a strong supporter of the development effectiveness agenda, grounded in country ownership, inclusive partnerships, focus on results, and mutual accountability and transparency. This September, Korea will host the Busan Global Partnership Forum to help implement FFD4 outcomes and mobilize coordinated action across stakeholders. Looking ahead, the FFD4 outcome document should provide clear and actionable guidance. Careful consideration is needed for proposals still at an early stage to ensure visibility and consensus. In a resource-constrained environment, we should build on existing platforms, leveraging their expertise in close cooperation with the UN system. In closing, FFD4 must deliver concrete, forward-looking commitments to close financing gaps and revitalize global partnerships for achieving the sustainable development goals. Korea stands ready to work constructively with all partners to this end. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea. I give the floor to
the representative of Cote d'Ivoire.

Thank you, Chairman. Chairman, I'd like to express my gratitude to the co-facilitators and all member states who are invested in preparing for the Seville conference, particularly the African group and the G77 plus China, with their various contributions to the process. We welcome the convening of the Seville Conference, which will provide a global platform to discuss current issues and to adopt ambitious resolutions to respond to global financing challenges at a time when international solidarity is in jeopardy in various domains, be it pertaining to development, trade, climate or humanitarian assistance. This state of affairs is undermining the efforts of the UN. and its capacities to help Member States to ensure greater that they have greater autonomy in their economy. Mr. President, like many countries in Africa, Cote d'Ivoire is committed currently to drafting a national development plan for 2026, 2030, which will have to see how we can overcome challenges pertaining to terrorism and violent extremism and cross-border crime. In terms of our regional commitments, notably our efforts under leadership of our president to implement the 2063 agenda of the African Union. We are trying to strengthen our partnerships and also working on strengthening the partnership between the AU and the UN. This partnership covers the implementation of the SDGs and the 2030 agenda and the pact for the future, and it allows us to address climate change, which is a major threat to development in Africa. In the context of this conference, my delegation welcomes the seven domains of action that have been identified, but the political message which must accompany these discussions around these inclusive matters is that international cooperation for development and trade is to the benefit of all. Guaranteeing transformative financing from the private sector with new technologies in an equitable trade framework can only be beneficial for global growth and global well-being. We're therefore convinced that the establishment of a new framework for financing will require robust strategic partnerships between governments, multilateral institutions, public and private investors and civil society to boot. These partnerships are critical to mobilize capital, to facilitate trade and to develop a prosperous, innovative global economy. In conclusion, we would like to reaffirm Cote d'Ivoire's commitment to the principles of sustainable development through the FFD4 and we intend to play our full part to ensure that the conference is successful.

Thank you.

Thank you so much. The next speaker is Chile. Thank you.

Your Excellencies, we endorse the statement delivered by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and China, and we'd like to make the following comments on our national capacity. We are grateful to the chairs, the co-chairs, and we welcome the efforts that have been made in the context of this process, and we need to have a transformative, agile new system. We are convinced that the fourth international conference on financing for development is not just a technical response to the financing challenges, it is a reaffirmation of multilateralism as the indispensable tool to allow us to make headway in achieving sustainable development. We need to establish a innovative framework and this is a critical moment. The crisis of sustainable development is real and urgent. The SDGs are badly off track and we need to focus on getting back on track. In this context, a new framework cannot be just technical in terms of how it is tweaked. It must really respond by providing a robust roadmap to allow us to make headway. In particular, middle income countries continue to face A structural contradiction, dependence on GDP per capita as the only measure has overlooked complex matters such as low productivity or our exposure to climate change. And that is why we welcome the fact that the first draft of the outcome document recommends, or recognizes rather, the specific needs of our countries through a robust technical process with inclusive participation within the context of the United Nations. We also need to make headway in achieving great representation for developing countries within the process. We need to improve how SDRs are channeled and we need to establish new ways of mobilizing resources, including innovative mechanisms and models that prioritize sustainability, inclusion and wellbeing. Chile strongly believes that the Seville Conference can mark a turning point if we can act with a vision of the future and if we commit to recover the centrality of sustainable development in the international agenda. At a time when fragmentation threatens global cooperation, let us make headway within this innovative framework. This would be a powerful sign that multilateralism remains our best tool to build a common future that leaves no one behind. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Chile for her statement.

To the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chairperson. Developing countries face a profound sustainable development crisis, with some SDGs standing off track and the financing gap being on the rise. In this context, CEBL must mark a turning point by deliberating on concrete collective action to address the imbalance. Tanzania joined other member states in emphasizing the need for a renewed financing framework and stressed that the framework should rest on three pillars, scaled up equitable international financing, reformed global financial governance, and strengthened domestic resource mobilization. These pillars can be elaborated through concrete actions required to achieve a more just and effective global financial system. First, multilateral development bank must significantly expand concessional financing and crowd in private capital through blended finance guarantees and risk sharing instrument. Second, a structured international financial architecture must include a rule-based sovereign debt mechanism, fairer credit rating systems, and voice for developing countries in global financial institutions. Third, developing countries must be supported in widening their fiscal space through technology transfers, capacity building, and fair and inclusive international tax architecture, including addressing tax evasion and illicit financial flows in order to ensure tax is paid where value is created. Civil must deliver on two critical outcomes, a clear roadmap for SDG investment surge with target for public and private invest flows and must end a commitment to governance reform. This is not just about bridging a financing gap. It is about restoring trust, enabling resilience, and securing a livable future for developing countries in particular. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Tanzania for her statement, and I will now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cape Verde.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Cape Verde aligns with the statement previously made by the G77 and China and EOSIS. In our national capacity, we'd like to make the following remarks. Cabo Verde, as a small island developing state, sits, remains firmly committed to advancing the financing for development agenda. As we approach the fourth international conference, we must be bold in addressing critical issues. Most notable, the need for sustainable development model supported by financing, a financial architecture that reflects today's realities, opportunities and challenges. States continue to grapple with the high debt burdens, limited fiscal space and exposure to external shocks. Sorry. Like economic, climate related and geopolitical shocks. Yet traditional criteria for concessional financing and development cooperation do not adequately reflect our structural vulnerabilities and the need for resilience building. We therefore reiterate our call for the urgent need of adoption of vulnerability and resilience indicators, such as multidimensional vulnerability index, as guiding tools for ensuring access to affordable and predictable financing based on actual exposure and the resilience building needs. We also underscore the importance of scaling up innovative financing instruments, including debt for development swaps, blue and green bonds, blended finance, and loss and damage mechanisms. These tools must be made accessible to SIDS and tailored to our national sustainable development priorities. Finally, we highlight the Antigua and Barbuda agenda for SIDS called ABAS. as a transformative blueprint to the next decade. Financing its implementation will require a renewed global compact rooted in equity, solidarity, and shared responsibility. FFD4 must be a turning point. Let us seize the opportunity to deliver concrete outcomes to create resilience and promote sustainable development.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cape Verde. The next speaker is Uruguay.

Thank you very much, co-facilitator. It's an honor for Uruguay to take part in this meeting. At a time that requires bold decision-making, we align ourselves with what was said by Spain on behalf of the Ibero-American community, distinguished delegations. Almost 10 years since the adoption of the 2030 Agenda and the SDGs, we remain committed to attaining them, convinced that only through multilateralism can we overcome the challenges that we are all facing. The fourth Financing for Development Conference in Seville is happening at a time when there are increasing geopolitical tensions, a climate crisis, increasing inequalities and… a worrying diversion away from the path towards sustainable development. The $4 trillion financing gap is not just a figure, it represents persistent inequalities. We think we need to undertake a root and branch reform of the international financial architecture to facilitate access for developing countries to concessional financing and to international cooperation bearing in mind their specific vulnerabilities and not just their income level. Our agreements should allow for resources to be oriented to achieving social justice and to protect global public goods. We must have a global investment strategy to channel resources towards projects that are aligned with the SDGs, particularly the energy transition. We think that we need to work on all of these issues. We reaffirm our support for these negotiations. We need to build bridges to bring us towards a new framework, building on the foundations of the Addis Ababa agenda to reach bold solutions focused on people and their rights, to get rid of the barriers that are today limiting, preventing developing countries from implementing their commitments. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Uruguay.

Despite these strong commitments made by member states to address these specific issues, the elements paper of the fourth international conference on financing for development recognizes that gaps remain in access to affordable financial services. In accordance with these commitments undertaken by member states, we recommend the following. One, that member states must take bold, Decisive action towards strengthening a comprehensive system that prioritized migrant youth in the outcome document. Two, ensure the provision of financial services for migrants and their family, both at home and abroad. Three, ensure that migrants are recognized appropriately in the outcome document. based on our multidimensional contributions to society. In conclusion, forced migration has become an increasing global crisis affecting young people who are compelled to flee their homes due to conflict, poverty, political oppression, discrimination, environmental threats, among others. Therefore, implementations of our recommendations and key policies are crucial to improving the lives of migrant youth.
